name: Reinsurance site selection maps
blurb: How reinsurers price seismic, coastal surge and grid vulnerability by geography.
summary: How reinsurers price seismic, coastal surge and grid vulnerability by geography.

part_3_high_value_red_flags: An absolute earth movement exclusion that removes all coverage for earthquake, landslide, and subsidence, leaving the insured with no seismic protection.
A flood exclusion that includes storm surge and tsunami, which would eliminate coverage for the most likely coastal loss scenario.
A named windstorm or hurricane deductible that applies as a percentage of total insured value rather than a fixed dollar amount, making small losses unrecoverable.
A sublimit for earthquake and flood combined that is far below the probable maximum loss, such as 5 million dollars when the PML is 100 million dollars.
A power outage or off premises utility failure exclusion that bars business interruption claims when the grid fails even if the insured site is undamaged.
A contingent business interruption exclusion that removes coverage for losses caused by damage to suppliers or customers in the same region.
A waiting period for business interruption of 30 days or more for earthquake or flood, which would eliminate most claims because restoration often takes longer but revenue loss starts immediately.
manuscript_wording_and_carve_backs: Negotiate a buyback of earthquake and flood sublimits to match the probable maximum loss, with separate sublimits for storm surge and tsunami rather than a combined cap.
Amend the earth movement exclusion to cover only land slippage and subsidence, while expressly including earthquake shock and fire following earthquake.
Add a contingent business interruption endorsement that covers loss of income when the public power grid fails for more than 72 hours, regardless of physical damage at the insured site.
Define occurrence for earthquake as all shocks within a 168 hour period, so aftershocks are treated as one loss and do not erode multiple retentions.
Include a service interruption clause that covers loss of revenue when the insured cannot provide utility services due to damage to transmission lines outside the site.
Negotiate a percentage deductible for earthquake and flood based on a per location value rather than total insured value, to avoid unaffordable retentions on large portfolios.
Add a reinstatement provision that allows one full reinstatement of the catastrophe limit for a second event in the same policy year, with a pro rata additional premium.

part_4_program_structure_and_limits.bi_waiting_period: Business interruption waiting periods for earthquake and flood are commonly 72 hours, but some reinsurers push for 168 hours or longer to reduce frequency of small claims.
part_4_program_structure_and_limits.business_interruption: Business interruption coverage for infrastructure is usually written on an actual loss sustained basis with a 12 month indemnity period, but extended period of indemnity for grid restoration can be negotiated up to 24 months.
part_4_program_structure_and_limits.property_eb_equipment: Equipment breakdown coverage for critical infrastructure is often sublimited to 10 million to 25 million dollars per occurrence, with separate deductibles for turbine, transformer, and switchgear failures.
part_4_program_structure_and_limits.per_occurrence_primary_excess_layered_pr: Property catastrophe reinsurance for infrastructure portfolios is typically structured in layers, with a primary layer covering losses up to a retention of 10 million to 25 million dollars, then excess layers in bands of 25 million, 50 million, and 100 million up to the probable maximum loss.

part_2_paper_type_and_limit_structure.cgl_primary: Typical primary commercial general liability limits for infrastructure owners are 1 million dollars per occurrence and 2 million dollars in the aggregate, but higher limits are often purchased for large public projects.
part_2_paper_type_and_limit_structure.paper_basis: Occurrence based applies here because property damage from seismic, coastal surge, or grid failure is a sudden and identifiable event with a clear date of loss, not a gradual or late reported claim.
part_2_paper_type_and_limit_structure.excess_umbrella_towers: Excess liability towers for infrastructure portfolios commonly stack in layers of 5 million, 10 million, and 25 million up to 100 million or more, with each layer attaching above the underlying limit.

part_1_core_third_party_liability_exposu: Bodily injury or property damage to third parties from structural collapse or falling debris during an earthquake or storm surge event.
Liability for damage to neighboring properties caused by ground movement, vibration, or water diversion from the insured site.
Environmental liability from release of hazardous materials stored on site when seismic or flood damage breaches containment systems.
Liability arising from failure of critical infrastructure such as power generation or water treatment that causes downstream economic losses to communities.
Claims from tenants or business invitees for injuries sustained during evacuation or shelter in place orders following a catastrophic event.
Product liability or professional liability if the insured provides engineering or site selection services to others and a map error leads to loss.
Directors and officers liability if inadequate risk mapping or disaster planning is alleged to have caused shareholder losses.

underwriter_wants_to_know: Precise geographic coordinates and site elevation for each insured location, including distance to mapped fault lines and coastal surge zones.
Construction type, year built, and seismic retrofit status for each structure, because older unreinforced masonry drives higher earthquake loss estimates.
Soil classification and liquefaction potential at each site, as soft soils amplify seismic shaking and increase foundation damage.
Flood zone designation and base flood elevation for coastal and riverine sites, including whether the site is inside a 100 year or 500 year floodplain.
Dependence on external power grids and presence of on site backup generation, because grid vulnerability affects both property damage and business interruption duration.
Historical loss experience for the portfolio by peril, including any past earthquake, flood, or wind losses at the same or nearby locations.
Maximum foreseeable loss and probable maximum loss estimates for the portfolio under different return periods, as these drive reinsurance pricing.
